extraction.name: Natural Questions
extraction.description: A question-answering corpus pairing real anonymized, aggregated Google search queries with Wikipedia pages and human annotations of long and short answers, including null answers when no suitable answer is present. It contains 307,373 training examples, 7,830 development examples, and 7,842 sequestered test examples.
extraction.creator: Google Research
extraction.citeAs: Tom Kwiatkowski, Jennimaria Palomaki, Olivia Redfield, Michael Collins, Ankur Parikh, Chris Alberti, Danielle Epstein, Illia Polosukhin, Jacob Devlin, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova, Llion Jones, Matthew Kelcey, Ming-Wei Chang, Andrew M. Dai, Jakob Uszkoreit, Quoc Le, and Slav Petrov. 2019. Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 7:453–466. https://doi.org/10.1162/tacl_a00276.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions were sampled from anonymized, aggregated Google search queries containing at least eight words and issued by multiple users within a short period. Linguistic heuristics filtered for likely factual questions. Each retained query was run through Google search and paired with its highest-ranked Wikipedia page, provided that page appeared among the top five search results. Human annotators then identified long and short answers on the page.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: User-generated content data, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine and complete Wikipedia pages appearing among the top five search results for those queries.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Source queries are described as anonymized and aggregated. Questions were randomly split into training, development, and test sets. Every question is unique under exact string matching. Test data were sequestered.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries were restricted to eight or more words and filtered using five linguistic heuristics involving question openings, verb forms, entities, modifiers, and categorical noun phrases. Categorical noun phrases were predefined using Hearst patterns to identify hypernyms; part-of-speech tags and entities were identified using Google's Cloud NLP API. Queries without a Wikipedia page among the top five search results were discarded. Examples without annotated answers were retained.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Around 50 annotators used a custom interface, with an average annotation time of 80 seconds. Each annotator completed three stages in succession. First, without seeing the Wikipedia page, the annotator classified the question as good or bad; bad questions included ambiguous, incomprehensible, false-presupposition, opinion-seeking, or non-factual requests. For good questions, the annotator selected the earliest suitable HTML bounding box containing all information needed to infer the answer, using the smallest sufficient paragraph, table, table row, list, or list item. A null long answer was assigned when no suitable single element existed. For non-null long answers, the annotator selected one or more short-answer spans, marked yes or no, or indicated that no short answer was possible. Comprehensive guidelines were developed and annotation quality was continuously monitored.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Four experts who prepared the annotation guidelines independently evaluated sampled non-null answers, then discussed disagreements to reach consensus judgments of Correct, Correct but debatable, or Wrong. Correct but debatable answers were counted as correct for precision, producing estimated long-answer precision of 90% and short-answer precision of 84%. Analysis of 25-way annotations examined disagreement over answer presence, passage location, and short-answer boundaries; much disagreement reflected genuine ambiguity or multiple acceptable answers. Evaluation uses five reference annotations: an answer is required when at least two annotators provide a non-null answer, and the prediction must match at least one reference annotation; otherwise a null prediction is required.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: One annotation per training example; five annotations per development and test example; 25 annotations per example for a separate analysis of 302 examples.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Google's Cloud NLP API identified part-of-speech tags and entities for query filtering. Answer annotations were created by humans.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors describe open-domain question answering as having significant utility to users and argue that solving Natural Questions would support useful information-seeking applications while driving advances in natural language understanding.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The authors explicitly acknowledge possible biases from using Wikipedia as the evidence source. Sampling focuses on queries of at least eight words because longer queries are considered more complex; the filtering heuristics generally exclude questions beginning with 'how to'.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Coverage is restricted to longer queries with a Wikipedia page among the top five Google search results. Answers requiring information spread across multiple allowed HTML elements receive null labels. Naturally occurring questions can have ambiguous answerability, multiple valid long answers, and substantial variation in short-answer boundaries. Expert evaluation estimated that 10% of non-null long-answer annotations and 16% of non-null short-answer annotations were wrong. In the development set, 79% of Wikipedia pages also occur in the training set.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Large-scale training, development, and testing of question-answering systems; research in natural language understanding; and study of human annotation variability. Models receive a question and an entire Wikipedia page and predict a long answer or null, plus a short answer where applicable. Evaluation uses the paper's five-annotation metrics, including precision, recall, and F1. The test set is sequestered.
